newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa gears up for bond market-makers in 1998.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa gears up for bond market-makers in 1998.

text.p: A major overhaul of the South African bond market, including the introduction of rolling settlement, will facilitate government's appointment of market-makers in its debt in 1998.
And once complete, analysts believe the reforms will place the country on a par with international standards, which will help develop other facets of the domestic market.

Government first mooted plans to appoint market-makers in March last year as part of the overall restructuring of its debt management and to remove what it has termed a conflict of interests with the central bank's role as monetary authority.
At present the Reserve Bank is the government's sole appointed market-maker.
A recent workshop attended by the Department of Finance, the Reserve Bank and market participants outlined issues that would need to be addressed before market-makers were appointed.
Chief among these issues, says Standard Bank's director of fixed interest Mike Lamont, is the introduction of a shorter settlement period.
"A prerequisite for the further development of the market in general and specifically for the reduction of credit exposures, will be a shorter settlement period," Lamont says.

South African traders currently deal for settlement on the second Thursday. That coupled with low margins encourages heavy speculative involvement which traders says reduces the spot market to a synthetic futures market.
Traders also believe that the current settlement procedure's non-conformity with international norms discourages foreign participation in the domestic market.
In a report to the Financial Markets Advisory Board, the Bond Exchange of South Africa highlighted a list of criteria that would need to be addressed before rolling settlement was introduced.
Among its pre-requisites are a developed futures market, a fully functional central depository with electronic settlement, and a developed repo market.
The exchange already has a fully functional central depository which has been successfully utilised in the electronic nett settlement process since October 1995.
Although a significant proportion of the major bonds traded in the market have been immobilised, traders believe that further progress needs to be made on this front.
The issues of developing the futures market and repo market, however, are expected to occur naturally as rolling settlement is introduced.

"T+3 will naturally force the speculators across to the futures market because they will no longer have this artificial future that they have had in the spot market," says Eric Wood, chief bond trader at Investec Merchant Bank. "I see the futures market mushrooming in a large way."
The South African Futures Exchange already offers bond futures but trade is extremely thin.
The same applies to the repo market. A shorter settlement period would mean traders had a shorter-time span to cover their positions, resulting in heightened liquidity on the repo market.
The reforms are expected to result in a dramatic reduction in liquidity on the spot market, a factor which is highlighted by opponents of the reforms.
Wood believes, however, that this will be more than compensated for by the expected explosion in liquidity on the futures market.
Potential market-makers have also voiced concern about what they term the regular leaking of market sensitive statistics to selective market players.
Analysts believe this problem could best be solved by the relevant authorities employing an independent auditing firm to introduce a stringent set of control measures.
Bond traders are optimistic that the introduction of "T+3" could be implemented as soon as July, subject to various logistical issues being resolved.
Once implemented, analysts believe the reforms will lead to greater foreign participation, while also allowing for South Africa's increased inclusion in international bond indices.
